nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the domestic epic and Catholic devotional verse
literary_identity: Poet and essayist; the poet of Victorian marriage and domestic love, whose long poem The Angel in the House gave the age its image of the wife.
biography: Born at Woodford, Essex, on 23 July 1823, the son of the writer Peter George Patmore; he was educated privately and at the British Museum, and worked for eighteen years in the printed books department of the Museum. He married Emily Andrews in 1847; her death in 1862 and his second marriage to Marianne Byles shaped his later verse. The Angel in the House (1854-62) made him famous and gave Victorian England its ideal of the domestic woman; after his conversion to Rome in 1864 his poetry became increasingly mystical, culminating in The Unknown Eros (1877). He died at Lymington on 26 November 1896.
literary_profile: Patmore is the poet of marriage as a sacrament: The Angel in the House is a long domestic epic, deliberately plain and conversational, which idealises the wife as the moral centre of the home and made the phrase 'the angel in the house' a permanent description of the Victorian ideal. His later odes in The Unknown Eros are among the most daringly irregular and mystical poems of the century, and his essay 'The Poetry of the Future' is a remarkable piece of prophetic criticism.
stylistic_characteristics: Conversational narrative verse in the plain style; the domestic detail; the ode with irregular, long-breathed stanzas; mystical eroticism; the deliberately unpoetic vocabulary of hearth and household.
intellectual_concerns: Marriage and domestic love as a religious state; the wife as the angel of the home; the education of the affections; Catholic mysticism and the love of God; death, bereavement and the afterlife; the relation of the sexes.
historical_significance: The Angel in the House created the Victorian ideal of the domestic woman and is therefore one of the most historically important poems of the century, the text against which the whole feminist critique of Victorian marriage was written. The Unknown Eros is a major achievement in its own right, admired by Hopkins and by the modernists.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the social novel, the historical romance and children's fantasy
literary_identity: Clergyman, novelist and poet; the leading voice of Christian Socialism and of 'muscular Christianity'.
biography: Born at Holne, Devon, on 12 June 1819, the son of a clergyman; educated at King's College London and Magdalene College, Cambridge. He was curate and then rector of Eversley, Hampshire, from 1844, and became a canon of Chester (1870) and Westminster (1873). He was a founder of the Christian Socialist movement with F. D. Maurice and J. M. Ludlow, wrote the social novels of the 1840s-50s, was a keen naturalist and sanitarian, and became Regius Professor of History at Cambridge in 1860. He died at Eversley on 23 January 1875.
literary_profile: Kingsley wrote the Victorian novel of social conscience as a Christian vocation: Yeast and Alton Locke exposed the condition of the agricultural labourer and the Chartist tailor, while Hypatia and Hereward the Wake made the historical romance a vehicle for a muscular, imperial Protestantism. He is also the author of The Water-Babies, one of the strangest and most inventive of English children's books, in which a chimney sweep's death becomes a fable of sanitation, evolution and redemption.
stylistic_characteristics: Direct moral address; documentary detail of poverty and disease; vigorous narrative action; natural history as moral illustration; a romantic, rhetorical prose; poetry of the sea and of the Christian year.
intellectual_concerns: Christian socialism and the condition of England; sanitation and public health; Chartism and working-class education; the relation of science and faith; empire and the English character; childhood and education.
historical_significance: Kingsley was the most influential Christian Socialist writer of the 1850s and the origin of the 'muscular Christianity' that shaped the Victorian public school and the imperial romance. Alton Locke is a founding text of the English working-class novel, and The Water-Babies is a permanent classic of children's literature.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Scottish; fantasy, the fairy tale and the Scottish novel
literary_identity: Novelist, poet and Congregational minister; the founding father of modern fantasy and the greatest Victorian writer of the fairy tale.
biography: Born at Huntly, Aberdeenshire, on 10 December 1824, the son of a farmer; educated at King's College Aberdeen and at Highbury College, London, he was minister of a Congregational church at Arundel from 1850 until his unorthodox views on hell forced his resignation in 1853. He supported himself by writing and lecturing, moved to Manchester and then to London, and from 1872 made several reading tours of the United States. He wrote over fifty books, including the Scottish novels of the 1860s, the fairy romances and the adult fantasies Phantastes and Lilith. He died at Ashtead, Surrey, on 18 September 1905.
literary_profile: MacDonald wrote the fairy tale as a form of theology: his fantasies proceed from the premise that the imagination is the organ of spiritual knowledge, and his stories of death, resurrection and the journey of the soul are the direct ancestors of the modern fantasy. He is also the finest Scottish novelist of rural life after Scott, and his portrayal of the Calvinist peasantry in David Elginbrod, Robert Falconer and Sir Gibbie is unmatched.
stylistic_characteristics: Dream-vision narrative; allegory carried by concrete imagery rather than abstraction; Scottish dialect speech; the kindly, unhurried narrator; the fairy-tale logic of transformation and redemption; a theology of universal love.
intellectual_concerns: The love of God and the possibility of universal salvation; death and the afterworld; the imagination as spiritual faculty; Scottish Calvinism and the peasant community; childhood and education; poverty and charity.
historical_significance: MacDonald is the founding figure of modern fantasy: C. S. Lewis called Phantastes the book that baptised his imagination, Tolkien and Chesterton acknowledged the debt, and Lilith and The Princess and the Goblin are permanent classics. His Scottish novels are a major achievement of nineteenth-century regional fiction, and his theology of universal love was one of the most original religious positions of the century.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the children's story and the family chronicle
literary_identity: Writer for children; one of the finest Victorian authors of the domestic children's story and a central figure of the golden age of children's literature.
biography: Born Juliana Horatia Gatty at Ecclesfield, Yorkshire, on 3 August 1841, the daughter of the clergyman and naturalist Alfred Gatty and the writer Margaret Gatty. She was educated at home and wrote stories for her mother's magazine, Aunt Judy's Magazine, which she later edited. She married Alexander Ewing, an army officer, in 1867 and travelled with him to Canada, Malta and India, writing her best stories in the intervals. She died at Bath on 13 May 1885.
literary_profile: Ewing wrote the children's story as a form of moral education without moralising: her children are real, quarrelsome, funny and often unhappy, and her plots turn on the ordinary crises of family life — a lost toy, a broken promise, a move to a new country. Her Canadian and Indian stories are among the first English children's books about the imperial experience, and her fairy tales and her novel The Story of a Short Life are still read.
stylistic_characteristics: Domestic realism with a child's-eye view; dialect and family idiom; gentle comedy; practical detail of toys, games and housekeeping; the family chronicle; the story shaped around a single moral problem.
intellectual_concerns: Childhood, obedience and self-knowledge; family life and the sibling world; emigration and the imperial family; illness and death; the natural world and the country year; the education of the affections.
historical_significance: Ewing is one of the great Victorian writers for children: her stories were admired by Ruskin and by the next generation of children's writers, and her Canadian and Indian tales are founding texts of the imperial children's book. Aunt Judy's Magazine, which she edited, was one of the most important nurseries of Victorian children's literature.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the children's novel and the family story
literary_identity: Writer for children; the most popular English author of the family story in the last quarter of the nineteenth century.
biography: Born Mary Louisa Stewart in Rotterdam on 29 May 1839, where her father was a merchant; she was brought up in Manchester and educated privately in Switzerland and London. She married Major Richard Molesworth in 1861 and, after an unhappy marriage ended in separation, supported herself and her children by writing. She published her first children's book in 1877 and produced over a hundred books, including the Carrots and The Cuckoo Clock series. She died in London on 20 July 1921.
literary_profile: Molesworth wrote the children's novel of everyday family life: her children are neither angels nor monsters, her nurseries are full of real furniture and real quarrels, and her stories teach by example and affection rather than by sermon. Her fairy tales, especially The Cuckoo Clock, are among the finest Victorian fairy stories, and her portraits of the English nursery and its governesses are a permanent record of middle-class Victorian childhood.
stylistic_characteristics: Plain, unhurried narrative; realistic dialogue, including the speech of servants and nurses; the small domestic incident as plot; gentle fantasy accepted as ordinary; a kindly, ironic narrator.
intellectual_concerns: Childhood and the nursery; the family and the household; education and the governess; illness; the fairy tale as a form of consolation; the relation of the middle-class child to servants and to the poor.
historical_significance: Molesworth was the most widely read children's writer in England between 1877 and 1900, and her books formed the taste of a whole generation: The Cuckoo Clock and The Tapestry Room are classics of the Victorian fairy tale, and her domestic stories are a key source for the history of Victorian childhood.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the children's adventure story, the fantasy and the social tale
literary_identity: Writer and poet; the founder of the modern children's adventure story and one of the most influential children's writers in English.
biography: Born Edith Bland in Kennington, London, on 15 August 1858; she was educated in boarding schools in England, France and Germany, and married Hubert Bland in 1880. She supported the family by writing, and with Bland was a founder of the Fabian Society in 1884. She published verse, novels and journalism for adults, and from 1899 a series of children's books that transformed the genre. After Bland's death she married Thomas Tucker in 1917 and died at New Romney, Kent, on 4 May 1924.
literary_profile: Nesbit wrote children as they are: quarrelsome, resourceful, greedy and brave, in families that are short of money and long on invention. Her great innovation was to put the magic in the middle of an ordinary suburban household and to let the children talk their way through it, and her time-travel and Psammead stories are the direct ancestors of the twentieth-century children's fantasy. She was also a socialist and a feminist whose adult fiction and verse are sharper than her reputation suggests.
stylistic_characteristics: Conversational, ironic narration with direct address to the child reader; comedy of family quarrels; magic treated as a practical problem; precise suburban interiors; rapid, episodic plotting.
intellectual_concerns: Childhood and the family; magic and the everyday; time travel and history; poverty and class; the position of women and girls; empire and the English abroad; the pleasures and dangers of wishes.
historical_significance: Nesbit invented the modern children's adventure story: The Story of the Treasure Seekers, Five Children and It and The Railway Children changed what children's fiction could be, and her influence on C. S. Lewis, Edward Eager and J. K. Rowling is direct and acknowledged.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Scottish-English; the animal fantasy and the essay of childhood
literary_identity: Writer; the author of The Wind in the Willows and of the finest Victorian essays on childhood.
biography: Born in Edinburgh on 8 March 1859; his mother died when he was five and he was brought up by his grandmother at Cookham Dean in Berkshire, the river landscape of his books. He could not afford Oxford and worked from 1879 at the Bank of England, rising to secretary in 1898. He published Pagan Papers (1893), The Golden Age (1895) and Dream Days (1898), and The Wind in the Willows in 1908. He retired from the Bank in 1908, and died at Pangbourne on 6 July 1932.
literary_profile: Grahame wrote the English river as a paradise: The Wind in the Willows is at once a children's book, an elegy for the Thames landscape and a comedy of English social types — Mole the suburban clerk, Rat the river poet, Toad the landed egotist, Badger the country magistrate. His earlier essays on childhood, narrated by children who have outgrown the nursery, are the most delicate English writing of the 1890s on the loss of the child's world.
stylistic_characteristics: Lyrical descriptive prose; gentle irony and self-mockery; the animal fable as social comedy; the rhythm of the seasons and the river; dialogue that makes character through idiom and catch-phrase.
intellectual_concerns: The English landscape and the river; friendship and contentment; the loss of childhood; class and the English gentleman; the machine and the modern world (Toad's motor-car); escape and homecoming.
historical_significance: The Wind in the Willows is one of the permanent books of English childhood and one of the great English pastoral idylls; it has been read as a parable of English social life, of the loss of Eden and of the friendship of men, and it has never gone out of print. Grahame's essays on childhood are the finest prose of the aesthetic 1890s.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Pagan Papers (1893); The Golden Age (1895); Dream Days (1898); The Reluctant Dragon (1898, in Dream Days); The Wind in the Willows (1908); The Cambridge Book of Poetry for Children (editor, 1916); First Whisper of 'The Wind in the Willows' (posthumous, 1944).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the picture book and the animal tale
literary_identity: Writer and illustrator; the creator of the modern English picture book and one of the most important children's authors of the twentieth century.
biography: Born Helen Beatrix Potter in Kensington, London, on 28 July 1866 into a wealthy Unitarian family; she was educated at home by governesses and studied drawing and painting privately, becoming a skilled scientific illustrator and mycologist. She began making picture letters to the children of her former governess, and The Tale of Peter Rabbit was privately printed in 1901 and published by Warne in 1902. She bought Hill Top Farm in the Lake District in 1905 and became a sheep farmer and conservationist, leaving her land to the National Trust. She died at Near Sawrey on 22 December 1943.
literary_profile: Potter made the modern picture book: the small square format, the exact watercolour illustration on every spread, the plain and mischievous story in which animals behave like naughty children and are nearly eaten. Her scientific accuracy and her feeling for the Lake District landscape give the books a permanence that most Victorian children's fiction lacks, and her stories are among the first to treat the child reader as an intelligent equal.
stylistic_characteristics: Simple, concrete sentences; the illustration as half the narrative; the animal protagonist as child; exact natural history; the comic chase; a very English sense of danger held within a safe frame.
intellectual_concerns: Childhood disobedience and its consequences; animals and the natural world; the English countryside and its seasonal work; property, trespass and the boundaries of the farm; the small-scale domestic economy.
historical_significance: Potter invented the modern picture book and became the first children's author to control the whole design of her books, including format, illustration and typography; her twenty-three tales have sold in the hundreds of millions and she is one of the most important figures in the history of English children's literature.
